## Installation

> [!WARNING]
> T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:
>
> - Codex: install [Codex CLI](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli) and run `codex login`
> - Claude: install [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) and run `claude auth login`
> - Cursor: install [Cursor CLI](https://cursor.com/cli) and run `agent login`
> - Grok Build: install [Grok Build CLI](https://x.ai/cli) and run `grok login`
> - OpenCode: install [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) and run `opencode auth login`
> - Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use **Install Antigravity** and **Sign in with Google**. No CLI is required.
> - fx: install [fx](https://fx.sh) and run `fx login` on the machine running the T3 Code server ([setup guide](./docs/user/providers-fx.md))

### Command line

```bash
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex
```

Then run `t3` to start the server and open the local web app. `t3 service install` keeps it running in the background, `t3 update` moves to a newer release, and `t3 --help` has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run `npx t3@latest` instead.

### Desktop app

Install the latest version of the desktop app from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases), or from your favorite package registry:

#### Windows (`winget`)

```bash
winget install T3Tools.T3Code
```

#### Windows (`scoop`)

```bash
scoop install extras/t3code
```

#### macOS (Homebrew)

```bash
brew install --cask t3-code
```

#### Debian, Ubuntu (`.deb`)

Download the `.deb` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code/releases), then:

```bash
sudo apt install ./T3-Code-*.deb
```

#### Arch Linux (AUR)

Stable:

```bash
yay -S t3code-bin
```

Nightly:

```bash
yay -S t3code-nightly-bin
```

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under [`packaging/aur`](./packaging/aur).

#### Nix (nixpkgs)

```bash
nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code
```

The package is maintained in [nixpkgs](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/tree/nixos-unstable/pkgs/by-name/t3/t3code)
and includes the desktop app (`t3code-desktop`) and the `t3` command.
See [Nix installation](./docs/user/install.md#nix-nixpkgs) for NixOS configuration and updates.

## Installation (30-second setup) A plugin updates itself. [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/mattpocock/skills) copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice. ### 1. Get the skills
Claude Code ```bash claude plugin install mattpocock-skills@claude-plugins-official ``` Updates itself by default.
Codex ```bash codex plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills codex plugin add mattpocock-skills@mattpocock ``` Updates itself at startup.
GitHub Copilot (CLI and VS Code) ```bash copilot plugin marketplace add mattpocock/skills copilot plugin install mattpocock-skills@mattpocock ``` Then, once, add to `~/.copilot/settings.json`: ```json { "extraKnownMarketplaces": { "mattpocock": { "source": { "source": "github", "repo": "mattpocock/skills" }, "autoUpdate": true } } } ``` In VS Code, run **Chat: Install Plugin From Source** and enter `https://github.com/mattpocock/skills`. It updates daily.
Gemini CLI (manual updates) ```bash gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/engineering gemini skills install https://github.com/mattpocock/skills.git --path skills/productivity ``` Re-run both commands to update.
Any other agent, or editable files (manual updates) ```bash npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose ``` When the installer asks which skills to take, include `setup-matt-pocock-skills`. To update, run `npx skills@latest update`, and re-run `add` to pick up new skills.
### 2. Run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` In your agent, run it once per repo. It will: - Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe) - Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them (`/triage` uses labels) - Ask you where you want to save any docs we create ### 3. Bam - you're ready to go.
installCommands: npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills -a <agent>  # cursor, opencode, devin, windsurf, amp, pi; omit -a to choose

## Quickstart

This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and an NVIDIA API key (`nvapi-...`) from
[build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com).

1. Clone the repository and create `.env`:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
   cp .env.example .env
   ```

   Then set these values in `.env`:

   ```dotenv
   DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-...
   AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
   APP_URL=http://localhost:3000
   POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
   AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   ```

   Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
   each default password before you start it. `.env.example` also sets an API
   key per model role: replace each `nvapi-your-api-key-here` with your key, or
   delete those lines so they fall back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`.

2. Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in
   auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --wait postgres
   git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
   (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
     POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \
     uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)
   ```

3. Build and start the rest of the stack:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

4. Open <http://localhost:3000> and sign in with `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL` and
   `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. Go to **Settings → Semantic
   Compilation** and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
   immediately and reports **Semantic compilation is ready** when it finishes.

5. Ask a question in **Chat**:

   > What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania
   > in June 2015?

   The agent resolves *revenue*, *product*, and *state* to terms in the
   ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the
   query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it,
   so you can check the result against the source:

   ```text
   Answer:  Reve

## Quick Start

**Installing for someone as an AI agent?** Run `npx claude-mem install --runtime worker` on their computer in an interactive terminal (enable PTY in your shell tool). It first asks in the terminal which agents to set up and, for Claude Code, whether to disable native auto-memory (and whether to overwrite an existing install). Relay each question to the user and type their answer, or pass `--ide <id>` to skip the first one. Keep the installer running. When it prints **Continue setup in your browser**, open that URL in the user's browser if the installer hasn't already opened it. Let the user go through setup and make their own choices, including the usage-analytics question the installer may ask at the end. If you can't run an interactive terminal on their computer, give them the command to run locally.

```bash
npx claude-mem install
```

The installer finds the agents on your machine and asks which ones to set up. Then just start working: observations stream in from your first prompt, and your second session in a project opens with memory from the first. (Copilot CLI, Goose, Roo Code and Warp get memory search only, so their sessions don't add to it.)

The installer sets everything up first, then asks you to sign in to claude-mem in your browser (email magic link, no card required to sign in). Choosing the **claude-mem observer** then starts its **30 Day Free Trial** on a checkout page that asks for a payment method; once it completes, the installer saves your memory key. With the observer, memory runs off-plan, so you get up to 100% more usage from your plan. When the free trial ends, memory automatically falls back to your Anthropic plan unless you subscribe. After sign-in you pick your memory provider: the claude-mem observer, your own OpenRouter or Gemini key, or your Anthropic plan.

Prefer to skip the sign-in? Pass an explicit `--provider` flag, set `CLAUDE_MEM_ONLINE_OPTIN=false`, or run in CI/non-interactive shells — the installer completes without any account interaction.

Your memory lives in `~/.claude-mem` on your machine. Cloud sync is opt-in. Anonymous usage analytics are on by default; `npx claude-mem telemetry disable` turns them off ([what's collected](https://docs.claude-mem.ai/telemetry)).

Or install from the plugin marketplace inside Claude Code:

```bash
/plugin marketplace add thedotmack/claude-mem

/plugin install claude-mem
```

## Install

```
npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g
```

`-g` installs for every project; leave it off to install into the current one. Needs Node 18 or later. The browser checks (`sloplint --render`, screenshots) also need `npm i -g puppeteer-core` and Chrome; without them the static checks still run.

| Harness | Lands in | Invoke |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/hallmark` | `/hallmark <prompt>` or describe a new build |
| Codex CLI | `~/.agents/skills/hallmark` | `$hallmark <prompt>` or describe a new build |
| Cursor | finds the copies above | `/hallmark <prompt>` or describe a new build |
| OpenCode | finds the copies above | `/hallmark <prompt>` or describe a new build |

- **One harness only:** `npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g --agent claude-code` (or `codex`, `opencode`, `cursor`, `github-copilot`).
- **As a Claude Code plugin:** `/plugin marketplace add nutlope/hallmark`, then `/plugin install hallmark@hallmark` (invoked as `/hallmark:hallmark`).
- **From a clone:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/install.mjs` validates every theme and reference before it copies; `install-hook.mjs` adds an edit-time Floor check to Claude Code.
- **Lint any page:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/sloplint.mjs <file-or-dir> --render`.
- **If it does not fire on its own,** name it: *use hallmark to build ...*.

## Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- [Git](https://git-scm.com/)
- [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) — the native installer is recommended (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` also works, on Node.js 22+)
- [Python 3](https://www.python.org/) — reads `project.yaml` for every skill and hook; without it every setting silently falls back to its default
- Bash — runs every hook; built into macOS and Linux, and on Windows it comes with [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win)
- **Recommended**: [jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq/) (for hook validation)

Hooks fail gracefully if optional tools are missing — you just lose validation — with one deliberate exception: a commit that stages data JSON is blocked when there is no Python to validate it.

### Setup

1. **Clone or use as template**:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game
   cd my-game
   ```

2. **Open Claude Code in the project's root folder** (the one holding
   `CLAUDE.md` and `project.yaml`) and start a session:
   ```bash
   claude
   ```
   Starting it in a subfolder such as `src/` skips the project's hooks, deny
   rules and ask-first permission mode.

3. **Run `/start`** — the system asks where you are (no idea, vague concept,
   clear design, existing work) and guides you to the right workflow. No assumptions.

   Or jump directly to a specific skill if you already know what you need:
   - `/brainstorm` — explore game ideas from scratch
   - `/setup-engine godot 4.7` — configure your engine if you already know
   - `/project-stage-detect` — analyze an existing project
